Uniform Title: Nityākaulatantra Secondary Title: Nityātantra Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No. 2-226, Reel No. B26/21a
Description: A description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski:
This is the only manuscript that has been recovered of this Tantra, also known as the *Nityātantra*. Although it is only a few [folios] long and badly damaged...
The manuscript on these leaves, which certainly predates the tenth century,
constitutes an important testimony for the early worship of Tripurāsundarī as Tripurabhairavī. This goddess is known to...
The Kubjikā Tantras, which precede the emergence of the well-known Śrīvidyā tradition centered on the worship of the goddess Tripurāsundarī, developed from the pool of the Nityā Yoginīs as...
Most important among these is the Śrīcakra, her distinctive yantra, around which a group of sixteen Nityās is configured;
this fragment is therefore of special importance for the historian of [the tradition].
The Development of This Tradition. Notes: Revision 0: November 15, 2014.

Having placed the previously mentioned seat, which is a hexagon representing the fire-mandala,
[one should contemplate] the one situated in its center...
Her face was like a lotus, possessing beauty, splendor, and intoxicating grace.
Her external appearance was like that of a lotus stalk, yet she possessed full and elevated breasts.
*Puṣpacā* ...
*bījapūraka-ha* ...
*rāṃ raktāṃ raktāntā yata* ...?
Wearing a crown of matted locks, she who possesses the three eyes... [filling in the gaps],
she who produces red unguents and delights this entire world,
dwells in the forest.
Standing at his side with an arrow, she who was previously situated in Ananta pervades the wheel in this very form.
Hṛllekhā, Kledanī, Nandā, Kṣobhaṇī, and Madanāturā.
Free from dust and devoid of passion, she is full of nectar.
2a) She is possessed of wisdom.
Khe, Kalā, Drāvaṇī, and likewise the excellent Vegavatī—
these eleven goddesses of yours are known as the twelve Madanas.
O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, O slender-waisted one, one should worship the great wheel situated pervading the spokes and the intervals between them.
Who is the one who delights and honors him through his conduct?
By the power of the Tālanivāsinī, the women of the Nyāsa are agitated.
The first syllable is indeed her own name;
likewise, the movement of the foot of sovereignty [is established].
As for the Goddess, she wears red garments, and her eyes are red at the corners.
Afflicted by passion, she was honored with incense, garlands, and other offerings. * * * *? All [the goddesses] were present with all their eyes. * * * *? With incense, garlands, and so forth.
O auspicious lady, I shall now describe to you properly how one should perform the supreme meditation:
[she who is] like a *indragopaka* insect, established in her own state, moving according to her own will.
In the space of the sky [of the heart],
one should draw the letter *ṭa*, which is situated in the center, beginning with the vowel *e* and ending with *la*.
In the middle of the *ṛ* and *la*, there is the letter *ṣa*; it is the first of the *ṣa*-group, ending with *sa*, and is honored as the group of letters from *ṣa* to *sa*.
The first letter is *ṭa*, which is empty; at the end of the letter *ṭa* is *dhaka*.
From this, I shall bring forth the supreme Vidyā, the most excellent...
through the application of the arrangement of the wheel, she who causes all women to melt.
The one that causes increase.
The ten-syllable Vidyā, characterized by a single letter, bestows enjoyment and liberation;
it destroys poverty and [fulfills] all desires.
O Goddess, it is joined with the first of the *ṭa*-group and the first of the *ā*-group, not conjoined with the end of *bhā*,
and situated above *ccha* and *dya*.
The seed-syllable situated between *dha* and *sa*, with *ṣa* and *ha* positioned above its middle;
the second [syllable] ending in *yā* at the top, joined with the *bindu*, O Great Goddess.
The third seed-syllable is said to be differentiated by the sixth [vowel] with the letter *ya*, while the fourth is the letter *ka* and so forth, together with the bindu.
That which is situated in the middle of Kha (*kha*) and [conjoined] with Pha-anta (*pha*),
[is the seed-syllable]. That sixth [syllable], situated in the middle of Ṣa (*ṣa*), is not differentiated by Yā-anta (*ya*).

The eighth is the letter *ai*; the ninth is known as the middle of *ṛ* and *ḷ*. Taking the letter *pa* situated in the middle, joined with the letter *cha*, and conjoined with the middle of *ka* and *la*, this is my eleventh syllable.
The subduer of the thirty-three gods.
O slender-waisted one, this goddess is the Great Vidyā named Nityā;
she is indeed the primordial means of accomplishment from beginning to end.
Neither is there a primary illumination for this, nor is it illuminated by that;
after the illumination,
O Goddess, I shall extract Kāmadeva together with his arrows.
Joined with the bindu of the letter Pha, [it is] at the crown of the head... [illegible].
Having taken the letter situated between *ṛ* and *ḷ*, it stands above the letter *ka*.
This has been fully explained with the bindu; now listen, O Pārvatī, to the description of the arrows.
He spoke to him who had gone to the middle; thus the mantra-practitioner, always meditating and reciting, [attains]... 3b) ...always meditating and reciting, [attains]...
And also the mistress of the house.
If the excellent practitioner should desire it, he may bring the three worlds under his control.
By reciting [the mantra] at the secret place... through the path of the moon, she who was previously enjoyed shall become submissive.
Having brought that secret [mantra] into the heart, one should forcibly draw it forth;
within seven nights, the gods... [will be subdued].
His name is like that which ends with... [illegible] ...prakhya.
Moving as before toward the woman,
he [visualizes] the syllable *Dā* situated in the middle of that;
likewise, at the commencement of an undertaking, in paralyzing an army, or for the continuity of progeny.
Or else,

one should visualize everything as being like a black bee; as before, one should contemplate the digit of Śaṅkara situated in the center, and one should contemplate the person to be subdued as resting upon that support.
Having reduced it to pieces, he kills it without hesitation.
Then, a smoke-colored wheel, formed there,
rotating with great velocity, causes even mountains to be uprooted.
In this way, Śivā accomplishes other rites as well— those scattered throughout various tantras— as well as those found in other tantras.
Thus ends the chapter on the Nityākaula... [fragmentary]. Now I shall fully explain another practice that is difficult to find on earth, which has come down through tradition.
That which is called "separated by a finger" refers to the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) being either variegated or indeed split apart.
By means of the yoni-mudrā of a bride, one may bring [others] under control; indeed,
it is said that through the power of this mudrā, all women are brought into subjection and become agitated,
offering [themselves].
That should be performed by one endowed with the vow; [the vow... ?
6b) The vow is auspicious.
The practitioner, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, with eyes anointed with collyrium, [should perform] the worship of the feet... [and so forth].
With his mouth filled with betel-leaf, he was well-perfumed by the fragrance of incense.
Indeed, at the three junctions of the day, when [the world] is worshipped by the sun,
the gods and the wives of the asuras cause agitation for him alone.
Her pair of thighs was caressed by waves of laughter, while she was tormented by the tips of the arrows of the God of Love.
Even the celestial maidens are agitated; what need is there to mention others?
At the conclusion of one hundred and eight [recitations], one should discharge a single arrow.
Having thus recited [the mantra] five hundred times, one should release the five arrows;
she, pierced by the hook of desire and struck by the power of the arrows of love, becomes overcome with longing.
Within seven days, the mantra-practitioner shall bring her here, even if she were Arundhatī herself;
[he shall bring] the flood of rivers, the lofty ramparts, and those situated within the high city gates.
Even if one has transgressed the samayas, by going [to the deity] while well-guarded and joined with the vow and mudrā, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment.
A celestial maiden, as well as a nāga woman, a gandharva woman, a yakṣa maiden,
a sovereign vidyādhara woman, and likewise human women.
O Dear One, the groups consist of seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one.
By the power of the mantra of the vow, she becomes a servant within a month.
O Pārvatī, listen attentively as I shall now explain the sequence of mudrās.
Having placed the two hands facing each other with their fingers interlaced,
one should raise the two middle fingers so that they touch one another.
The two index fingers are firmly pressed together, while the ring fingers are properly bent; having made the two thumbs equal, the middle fingers and the little fingers [are likewise joined].
This is your mudrā of the womb, which bestows all things and causes agitation;
O slender-waisted one, rub your hands together with force until they form fists.
One should bind that very mudrā as before;

she is the goddess who causes great agitation. Therefore, she is exclusively [to be practiced] in solitude. By remembering the goddess through the red and non-red syllables, the world is repeatedly subdued.
Because it is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is situated above that.
The practitioner of mantra should visualize the red goddess; he shall become submissive like a servant.
Thus [ends] the Nityākaula... [fragmentary].
7b) The Goddess said:
The secret mantra, mudrā, and likewise the vows have been told;
now, O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me what the signs of realization are.
"O Vāha, tell me according to the truth.
Bhairava said:

The goddess, having entered a red thread, [is] a ruby... Thus she, having emerged from the red thread, [is] flowing forth as nectar... resembling the trunk of an elephant, having emerged, it enters the heart.
Having meditated upon [the deity] situated within the lotus of one's own heart, this supreme method of attraction is considered the best.
By covering the path of the sky and the worlds of the ten directions with that [light],
one attracts whatever it is that [is to be drawn].
One should visualize the blue thread as having become twofold, taking the form of two blue crows;
the second is in the shape of an owl, emerging from the Brahma[-aperture].
Having brought those two into the heart, one should then join them with the apāna.
O slender-waisted one,
O auspicious lady, if he does not abandon his yoga, he will become exceedingly beloved by both [the gods and the asuras].
One should visualize the mantra in the form of smoke;
impelled by that, the person to be acted upon is led toward the direction of the wind.
She swiftly uproots even that which is equal to Mount Meru;
for she, the Goddess who resembles a thread, completely envelops it from all sides.
The goal is perfectly stabilized therein;
the eternal Goddess, ever-luminous, completely fills the mouth [of the lotus]. She enters her own abode within the Kadamba forest.
One should conquer that which stands at the end of the Vidyā together with its emission (*visarga*);
one should enter with speed as it is emerging.
O Great Goddess, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, a man becomes an achiever of his purpose.
One should remember that thread—black for killing, white for pacifying, and yellow for the form of prosperity.
Or perhaps, out of compassion, he brings them back again.
The white thread, resembling a hundred moons,
flows with the surging foam of the dead;
even the nectar situated upon the head becomes [the source of] immortality.
In her roar, her voice, like a thunderbolt, cuts through the space between the jaws.
Or, having visualized the form as having the appearance of the sun, the wise one should pierce [it];
by doing so correctly, even Vācaspati would become liberated after a long time.
The threads of saliva, having become like the circle of the sky,
pierce the vital points of the limbs and enter their own abodes.
Having established the apāna for as long as it lasts, his success indeed declines;
there is no doubt about this. Now, the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) is being described.
Forming a stream of milk that enters the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one should accomplish this as taught by the Great One; it is the supreme bringer of all peace.
9a) The sixteenth digit (kalā), which resides in the heart and is as white as snow, kunda flowers, or the moon,
is joined with the Vidyā at the beginning and the end through the union of each individual syllable.
Emerging from the cave of the heart, she should flood the circle of space;
by recollecting the Goddess in this way for each [breath], one will become a conqueror of death within six months.
With a complete body, auspicious and pleasing to behold from every side,
he who has performed the fire-oblation, is learned in the scriptures, and has been initiated, attains success through the teachings.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Nityākaula.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, God of gods, please explain initiation (dīkṣā) in brief,
as well as the fire-ritual (agnikārya) according to the rules, along with the instruction for the consecration ceremony (sakautuka).
"What is the characteristic of the repeated utterance of the Goddess?
Bhairava said:
One who possesses good qualities and is endowed with integrity should first thoroughly examine the disciple.
First, however, one should draw a mandala made of rice-flour paste.
O you who have gone to the red sindūra, drink!
First, the hexagon was described according to the sequence beginning with worship.
Having covered it with red cloth, one who has attained the vidyā should employ it;
[the vessel] should be filled with a handful of red flowers and provided with red-colored food.
One should cause [the disciple] to cast [the seed-syllable] into the center of that; one should fashion the name ending with the Śakti.
Then, having established the locus of fire, the wise teacher should initiate [the disciple].
O Dear One, having prepared a pit marked with a lotus or according to one's desire,
it should be square for rites of pacification (śāntika) and circular for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
For malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the pit is triangular; for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is semi-circular;
O Goddess of the Gods, the lotus-shaped pit grants all desires.
Having resolved upon the inhalation there,
one should cause the cutting of the bonds by means of the mechanical enjoyment and so forth, O best of gods, at each and every level of reality (tattva).
One should first recollect the eleventh [syllable], which is born from the reverse order;
one should then remember the first word, beginning with the earthly element and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti).
Above that is the principle of Puruṣa, endowed with the three qualities;
the third is the principle of Niyati, and the fourth is the principle of Kāma.
The fifth is the principle of passion (rāga-tattva), while the sixth is known as ignorance (avidyā).
The seventh is indeed the principle of limited agency (kalā-tattva), and the eighth is traditionally called illusion (māyā).
The ninth reality is Vidyā, the supreme state of the Vidyeśvaras;
however, they know the eleventh to be both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
One should perform initiation for each individual syllable using the mantras proclaimed by Śiva;
then, with all the mantras, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to the Lord of Gods.
10a) Thus, O Goddess, one who is initiated shall obtain the fruit of all desires;
or, O Goddess, by a single utterance, [he attains it] from his place of birth up to Śiva.
Having perceived the meditation with the mind, the Tantra is eternally spread out;
the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) shall indeed be the initiation that bestows liberation.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one shall proceed to the state of Sadāśiva;
thus has been described the initiation into the great and formidable Ṣom, accompanied by its signs of realization.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, listen as I describe the fire-ritual (agnikārya) according to its true nature,
together with the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the consecration of the fire.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], the fire-oblation (homa) should be carried out, which bestows prosperity and leads to the supreme state;
if one should offer guggulu resin combined with camphor and agallochum, [the result is unsurpassed].
Upon reaching the state of a Vidyeśvara, one shall attain liberation at the end;
by abandoning Kāśmīra, one attains the status of Indra and becomes the lord of its enjoyments.
By performing a *homa* with red sandalwood and *kuśumbha* in the middle [mandala], O Great Goddess, one quickly becomes like the Candrabhāgā river.
By offering parched grain (*lājā*) into the fire, O Great Goddess, one becomes like the Candrabhāgā.
By performing a *homa* with *nāgakeśara* and *puṇṇāga*, one becomes a holder of the vidyās.
One should propitiate the Yakṣiṇīs with offerings of Kadamba and Bakula flowers;
by offering a hundred thousand Jāti flowers as oblations, one becomes a partaker of the enjoyments of the Gandharvas.
By offering oblations of *karavīraka* flowers, a woman shall become submissive; by offering *vaṃdhūka* and *kiṃśuka* flowers, she will certainly come under one's control.
Having offered flowers of the girikarṇika plant, the Brāhmaṇa indeed dwells in bliss.
The Kṣatriya is brought under control by offerings made with *kāmamardaka*;
the servants are indeed subdued by means of *māṣapannaka* for the Śūdras.
O Goddess of the Guru, the red lotus brings subjugation of courtesans, while the *va* [flower] brings subjugation of the king’s wife; the jasmine garland (*mālikā*) brings the subjugation of princes.
By offering *caṃpaka*, *pāṭala*, and other such flowers, one shall obtain prosperity (*śrī*).
With *priyaṅgu* and plantain flowers, one may bring all sentient beings under one's control. [One may also do so] with thick, fresh buds of *palāśa* and with auspicious sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.
O Pārvatī, the pacification of all calamities arises from the fire-oblation;
through those oblations of edible foods, drinks, and so forth, all prosperities are attained.
And whatever else there may be of meat, O Great Goddess, if it is drenched with honey and ghee, that becomes inexhaustible; there is no doubt in this regarding those who have attained the true path.
Through worship one obtains honor; through recitation, one does not fail to achieve success;
through fire-offerings, there is prosperity, good fortune, and the accomplishment of one's goals.
Having made meditation the condition and ensuring a well-provided collection of materials,
one should thus perform the renowned fire sacrifice (homa), and at the end, offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
O Great Goddess, ending with *vauṣaṭ*... [text missing] ... ||
Therefore, out of affection for you, I shall speak further instruction:
having reflected upon it, O breath, become free from thought, devoid of both thinking and the absence of thought.
O Pārvatī, I shall explain the instruction in its threefold form according to reality:
that which is accompanied by thought, that which is free from thought, and that which is devoid of both thought and non-thought.
O Dear One, having meditated upon fire, form, the bindu, and that which is called nāda,
one should then contemplate the object of meditation through the application of the syllables beginning with 'dā'.
Wearing a garland of flowers, radiant, and with a flower-bow raised, [she is] Rām.
The goddess Puṣpavāsinī, adorned with four hands,
was mounted upon a beautiful and excellent chariot in her divine form.
O Great Goddess, you are infinite and endowed with four lion-thrones; dharma, knowledge, and so forth, dispassion, and sovereignty are the lions upon your throne.
Mounted thereon was Madana himself, the driver of the chariot, whose mind was his own;
he was intent upon his flower-bow and arrows, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
The moon is situated in the center of the sun, and within that is the mandala of fire;
the goddess resides therein, both gentle and fierce.
Having visualized the name of the person to be accomplished situated within the heart— resembling a ruby and like the flickering of lightning— that is called meditation (dhyāna).
O beloved, that which is the cause through the yoga of meditation,
and which exists in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, is called both the conceivable and the inconceivable.
It should not be thought of even as the mind, nor does it exist apart from the thinker;
it is entirely free from all principles and devoid of all activity.
What is it? It is that which is devoid of instruments, actions, and forms such as color and so forth.
This excellent, pure, and inconceivable yoga has been spoken by you;
it includes both types of accomplishment as well as the signs of attainment therein.
Those ritual actions which correspond to the measures of reality—
this is declared to be the essence of the Nityātantra in brief.
This compendium of the Kaula tradition should never be given to a mere disciple nor even to one's own son; it should be given only to one who is devoted to the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire.
Otherwise, he who bestows [the teaching] would become a hell-being deprived of accomplishment;
for from giving it only after thorough examination arises the fruit of all accomplishments.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Nityākaula.
12a) The Goddess said:
Blessed One, everything that I have asked has been explained;
now speak of the section on the mechanical device, the path of yoga, which is full of wonder.
Bhairava said:
O dark-waisted one, out of affection for you, I shall first describe the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra:
the letter *ha* ending with a bindu, followed by *pa*, with *sa* situated in the middle, and then *ya*.
One should place the letter *śa*, which stands above the *upa* (the vowel *u*), and is endowed with the radiant (*bhānta*) [letter *ra*];
then, make the third letter *ka* situated in the middle of *ḷ*, joined with the *śṛṣṭi* (the vowel *e*).
O slender-waisted one, this triad, which is perfectly united with knowledge,
is the pacifier of great death and the destroyer of calamities.
O Great Goddess, having written one's own name together with [the mantra] on the arm or on the neck, O Supreme Sovereign,
its wearing shall be the conqueror of death.
When the immortal fuel (*amṛtā*) spoken of at the three junctions of the day lies upon the surface,
he is not capable of harming even a single hair of this [being].
O Great Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, Hṛllekhā is situated between the letters *cha* and *la*, with *ū* and *pha* positioned above the middle, and joined with the bindu.
But those joined with the letter *mā* attract the three worlds; it is conjoined with the letter *ṣa*. The reality situated in the middle is located above that which is to be concealed (*cchādya*).
One should perform the piercing with the letter *ha* ending in a nasal (*m*), joined with the bindu; this is the Great Hook (*mahāṅkuśa*).
By means of this, the practitioner brings the three worlds under control.
12b) Having taken the letter situated between *ṭa* and *ḍha*, it is pierced by the wind (*vādyena*).
The second [letter] is *pa* situated in the middle of *na*; at its end is the horse (*haya*) in the middle.
Place the letter situated in the middle of *ga* together with the creator of emanation (*śṛṣṭikṛt*).

O beautiful one, the process of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) has been proclaimed; by performing oblations, one attains peace, and having written [the mantra], it should be worn upon one's own body.
The immortalization is proclaimed as the nourishment for what has decayed; the seed-syllable situated between the letters Pha and Ja is the supreme neutralizer of poison.
The great seed-syllable beginning with the letter *e*, its beginning and end formed by the Vidyā,
joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and situated in the center of the circle of fire—
when combined with the Vidyā, O blessed one, it is used for paralyzing, burning, fevers, and the like.
And the supreme rite for subduing the base must be performed;
having taken that which is situated in the middle of the water, located within the mandala, and accompanied by the bindu.
This supreme rite of eradication (uccāṭana) is remembered as being joined with the Vidyā at its beginning and end;
it is performed while facing the northwest, with Kṛṣṇā and Kṛṣṇa worshipped with the appropriate offerings.
O beautiful one, one should place the seed-syllable in the center of the fruit, situated above the *śānta*;
he should make that bindu agitated among those joined with joy.
The Lord is eternally present among those who are filled with affection between husband and wife, as well as between master and servants;
there is no need for deliberation here regarding what causes supreme anger. Place the seed-syllable situated between *oṃ* and *ṭha*, and cause it to fall at the end.
O Dear One, having thus joined the seed-syllable situated in the middle as it proceeds, one should, at the end, include the visarga;
this shall slay even the gods.
Endowed with twelve digits and situated in the center of the solar orb, there is the blazing Kula of garlands of flames; in its midst is the Supreme Goddess.
Piercing all the vital points and reaching as far as the heart-center,
it produces a supreme state of paralysis when correctly recited by you.
The full moon disc, joined with the sixteen vowels,
resembling molten gold— may it indeed flow forth, not white.
The goddess Cintyā is the Great Goddess, the accomplisher of all desired aims;
whatever is wished for, she brings that very thing into manifestation through her contemplation.
Now, O beloved, this supreme essence, the Compendium of the Essence of Yoga,
must be kept secret by you in the Unnameable [Anākhye] and within the Yantra.
As many as there are lords of all yogas who have been obstructed in their Bhairava-form, so many times [the mantra] is recited; he who [performs this] in the heart [attains] great passion.
O fortunate one, I shall fully explain this Yoga to you, who have been malicious toward me and toward your gurus,
as long as the body remains supported by the tortoise.
five wheels
